parts.problem_md:
A mass-spring system has been set up horizontally on the lab bench, so that the mass can oscillate.

Sketch a velocity-displacement graph of the motion of the block as it undergoes simple harmonic motion.
parts.solution_md:
A graph which would score full credit is shown below:

![ma2b_oscillations_ib-sl-physics-sq-medium](assets/001-ma2b-oscillations-ib-sl-physics-sq-medium.png)

- When displacement $x$ = 0, velocity is maximum in both directions (the mass is in equilibrium); **[1 mark]**
- When velocity $v$ = 0, displacement is maximum in both directions (the mass is at its amplitude); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *You are unlikely to be given a question as tricky as this in your exam but being able to do it and follow the thought process will set you up well for other difficult questions. The thinking involved is not beyond that of a top A level candidate.*

> *The question is asking for a **velocity-displacement** graph and not a displacement graph.*

> *When sketching graphs, take it step by step. Start with the situation for one variable being zero – what is the other value at this point? Next walk through the motion. Sketching a drawing of the object in motion often helps. You might have been tempted to draw a sine wave in answer to this question, but that only applies when **time** is on the x-axis.*

> *The important fact to remember is that when **x** = 0, **v** = maximum and when **x** = maximum, **v** = 0.*

parts.problem_md:
A mass of *m* = 50 g is attached to the mass-spring system.

The graph in Fig. 1.1 shows the variation with time of the velocity of the block.

![q2c_oscillations_ib-sl-physics-sq-medium](assets/002-q2c-oscillations-ib-sl-physics-sq-medium.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Determine the total energy of the system when it is oscillating with a mass of 50 g.
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Mass attached to the spring, *m* = 50 g = 0.05 kg
- $E_{k}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ *mv*<sup>2</sup>

![ma2c_oscillations_ib-sl-physics-sq-medium](assets/003-ma2c-oscillations-ib-sl-physics-sq-medium.png)

- From the graph, $v_{max}$= 0.1 m s<sup>–1 </sup>

State that the total energy of the system is equal to the maximum kinetic energy:

- $E_{T}$ = $E_{Kmax}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the maximum kinetic energy, $E_{Kmax}$:

- $E_{Kmax}$ =  $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}_{max}$
- $E_{Kmax}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$$mv^{2}_{max}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ × 0.05 × (0.1)<sup>2</sup> = 0.25 mJ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *The total energy of the system at maximum velocity is equal to the maximum kinetic energy.*

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

A mass of m = 50 g is attached to the mass-spring system. The graph in Fig. 1.1 shows the variation with time of the velocity of the block. Fig. 1.1 [velocity-time graph: velocity oscillates sinusoidally, v_max = 0.1 m/s, with v = 0 at t = 0, 2, 4, 6 s]. Determine the total energy of the system when it is oscillating with a mass of 50 g. Mark scheme: E_T = E_Kmax = ½ × 0.05 × (0.1)^2 = 0.25 mJ

Determine the potential energy of the system when 6 seconds have passed.
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Maximum kinetic energy, $E_{k}$= 0.25 mJ (from part b)

Determine the equation for potential energy, $E_{P}$:

- The total energy of the system, $E_{T}$ = Kinetic energy,  $E_{k}$+ Potential energy $E_{P}$
- Therefore, $E_{P}=E_{T}-E_{K}$

  - When the kinetic energy is 0, the potential energy is at a maximum

Determine *v*  from the graph at *t* = 6 s:

- When$t$ = 6 s the velocity, $v$ = 0

  - This means $E_{k}$= 0 ![ma2d_oscillations_ib-sl-physics-sq-medium](assets/004-ma2d-oscillations-ib-sl-physics-sq-medium.png)

Determine potential energy, $E_{P}$:

- *v* = 0 at the maximum or minimum amplitude of the oscillation

  - This means all the kinetic energy has been transferred to potential energy
- Therefore $E_{P}=E_{T}$ = 0.25 mJ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

> *Some questions are easier than they look at first glance. Be aware that a question worth only 1 mark probably doesn’t have very much working required to answer it. Don't confuse the potential energy in this scenario with gravitational potential energy. *

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

A mass of m = 50 g is attached to the mass-spring system. The graph in Fig. 1.1 shows the variation with time of the velocity of the block. Fig. 1.1. Determine the total energy of the system when it is oscillating with a mass of 50 g.
From the graph, v_max = 0.1 m s^–1. The total energy of the system is equal to the maximum kinetic energy: E_T = E_Kmax = 1/2 m v_max^2 = 1/2 × 0.05 × (0.1)^2 = 0.25 mJ. Time period T = 4 s (from graph).

The mass-spring system is now fixed so the mass and spring oscillate vertically. The mass remains at 50 g and the angular velocity and time period the same as before.

Show that the total energy of the system is still the same as in part (b).
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- Mass, *m *= 50 g = 0.05 kg
- Total energy of system in part b), *E*<sub>*T*</sub> = 0.25 mJ
- Time period of oscillation, *T *= 4 s (from part b)
- *v*<sub>*max*</sub> = 0.1 m s<sup>−1</sup> (From part b)

Determine the angular velocity of the oscillation, *ω*:

- Recall: $ω=\frac{2π}{T}$
- $ω=\frac{2π}{4}=\frac{π}{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the amplitude of oscillation, *x*<sub>*0*</sub>:

- Recall: $v_{max} = ω x_{0}$
- $x_{0}=\frac{0.1}{\frac{π}{2}}=0.06366m$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the total energy of the system, *E*<sub>*T*</sub>:

- Recall: $E_{T}=\frac{1}{2}mω^{2}x_{0}^{2}$
- `E _ T = 1 half x 0.05 x ( pi / 2 ) ^2 x 0.06366 ^2 = 2.5 x 10 ^ - 4 = 0.25 mJ` **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *For a vertical mass-spring system, measuring displacement from the equilibrium position means gravitational potential energy is already accounted for. The total energy is still *`E_{T} = \frac{1}{2} m \omega^{2} \left(x_{0}\right)^{2}`* where *$x_{0}$* is measured from equilibrium.*

parts.problem_md: Define the total energy for a system oscillating in simple harmonic motion.
parts.solution_md:
The total of energy of a system oscillating in simple harmonic motion is:

- The <u>sum</u> of the <u>potential energy</u> and the <u>kinetic energy</u> of the system; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

> *You may also have answered this question using the equation **E*<sub>*T*</sub>* = **E*<sub>*p*</sub>* + **E*<sub>*k*</sub>*. This is ok as long as you remember to define the terms you use. For example, the total energy **E*<sub>*T*</sub>*  is equal to potential energy **E*<sub>*p*</sub>* plus kinetic energy **E*<sub>*k *</sub>*in a system.*

parts.problem_md:
Fig. 1.1 shows the positions of a simple pendulum in simple harmonic motion.

![4-1-4c-question-stem-sl-sq-easy-phy](assets/005-4-1-4c-question-stem-sl-sq-easy-phy.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Identify the position of the pendulum when:

(i) Kinetic energy is zero

[1]

(ii) Potential energy is at a maximum

[1]

(iii) Kinetic energy is at a maximum

[1]

(iv) Potential energy is zero

[1]
parts.solution_md:
(i) Identify the position of the pendulum when kinetic energy is zero:

- The kinetic energy is zero at amplitude *x*<sub>*0*</sub>
- Therefore, kinetic energy is zero at position A **OR** C **[1 mark]**

(ii) Identify the position of the pendulum when potential energy is at a maximum:

- The potential energy is at a maximum at the amplitude *x*<sub>*0*</sub>
- Therefore, potential energy is at a maximum at position A **OR** C; **[1 mark]**

(iii) Identify the position of the pendulum when kinetic energy is at a maximum:

- The kinetic energy is at a maximum at the equilibrium position
- Therefore, the kinetic energy is at a maximum position B; **[1 mark]**

(iv) Identify the position of the pendulum when potential energy is zero:

- The potential energy is zero at the equilibrium position
- Therefore, potential energy is zero at position B; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *You may want to annotate the diagram to help you visualise the energy transfers to help with your answer. *

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

(iii) Identify the position of the pendulum when kinetic energy is at a maximum:
- The kinetic energy is at a maximum at the equilibrium position
- Therefore, the kinetic energy is at a maximum position B

At the equilibrium position, the kinetic energy of the pendulum is 0.324 J.

Determine the total energy of the system.
parts.solution_md:
To determine the total energy of the system:

- The kinetic energy is at a maximum as the pendulum swings through the equilibrium position
- Maximum kinetic energy = total energy of the system;** [1 mark]**
- *E*<sub>k max</sub> = *E*<sub>total</sub> = 0.324 J **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

At the equilibrium position, the kinetic energy of the pendulum is 0.324 J. Determine the total energy of the system.
The kinetic energy is at a maximum as the pendulum swings through the equilibrium position. Maximum kinetic energy = total energy of the system; E_k max = E_total = 0.324 J

The amplitude of the pendulum is 5 cm, and the mass of the bob is 20 g.

Calculate the angular speed of the pendulum as it swings through the equilibrium position.
parts.solution_md:
Calculate the angular speed of the pendulum at the equilibrium position:

List the known quantities:

- Amplitude, $x_{0}$ = 5 cm = 0.05 m
- Mass, $m$ = 20 g = 0.02 kg
- Total energy, $E$ = 0.324 J

Use the equation for total energy in SHM and rearrange to make *ω* the subject:

- $E=\frac{1}{2}mω^{2}x_{0}^{2}$
- $ω=\sqrt{\frac{2E}{mx_{0}^{2}}}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in the known values to calculate:

- $\\omega = \sqrt{ \frac{2 \times 0.324}{0.02 \times ( 0.05 )^{2}} }$ **[1 mark]**
- $ω=113.84=114\mathrm{rad}s^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
Fig. 1.1 shows a mass-spring system which undergoes simple harmonic motion.

The mass of 75 g is connected between two identical springs. The mass-spring system rests on a frictionless surface. A force of 0.025 N is needed to compress or extend the spring by 1.0 mm.

The mass is pulled from its equilibrium position to the right by 0.055 m and then released. The mass oscillates about the equilibrium position in simple harmonic motion.

![9-1-hl-sq-medium-3a-mass-spring](assets/007-9-1-hl-sq-medium-3a-mass-spring.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Calculate the acceleration of the mass at the moment of release.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the acceleration at the moment of release:

List the known quantities:

- Mass,* m*<sub>*m*</sub> = 75 g = 0.075 kg
- Force per mm, *F* = 0.025 N mm<sup>−1</sup>
- Amplitude of oscillations, $x_{0m}$ = 0.055 m = 55 mm

Determine the force required to pull the mass 0.055 m to the right:

- Force = force per mm × amplitude of oscillation
- F = 0.025 × 55 = 1.4 N per spring
- There are two springs so 2 × 1.4 N = 2.8 N

Calculate the acceleration at the moment of release:

- Rearrange *F* = *ma*
- *a *=* *$\frac{F}{m}$* = *$\frac{2.8}{0.075}$* *= 37 m s<sup>−2</sup> **[1 mark]**

Consider the direction of motion:

- Since *a* ∝ −$x$, *a* will be negative
- *a* = −37 m s<sup>−2 </sup>**[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
The mass-spring system from part (a) can be used to model the motion of an ion in a crystal lattice structure. The model is shown in Fig. 1.2.

![9-1-hl-sq-medium-3a-ion](assets/008-9-1-hl-sq-medium-3a-ion.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

The frequency of the oscillation of the ion is 8 × 10<sup>12</sup> Hz and the mass of the ion is 6 × 10<sup>−26</sup> kg. The amplitude of the vibration of the ion is 2 × 10<sup>−11</sup> m.

Estimate the maximum kinetic energy of the ion.
parts.solution_md:
To estimate the maximum kinetic energy of the ion:

List the known quantities:

- Frequency, *f *= 8 ×10<sup>12</sup> Hz
- Mass of ion,* m*<sub>*i*</sub> = 6 ×10<sup>−26</sup> kg
- Amplitude of oscillations, $x_{0i}$ = 2 ×10<sup>−11</sup> m

From the data booklet:

- *K*<sub>*E*</sub> = $\frac{1}{2}$*mv*<sup>2</sup>
- $E=\frac{1}{2}mω^{2}x_{0}^{2}$

Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the ion:

- $K_{Emax}=E_{total}$
- $E=\frac{1}{2}mω^{2}x_{0}^{2}$ and $ω=\frac{2π}{T}=2πf$
- Combining these equations gives $E = 1 \frac{1}{2} m ( 2 \mathrm{\pi } f )^{2} x_{0}^{2}$
- $E = 1 \frac{1}{2} \times ( 6 \times 10^{- 26} ) \times ( 2 \mathrm{\pi } \times ( 8 \times 10^{12 ) )^{2} \times ( 2 \times 10^{-11} } )^{2}$** [1 mark]**
- $E = 3 \times 10^{- 20} \mathrm{J} ( 1 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
A small metal pendulum bob is suspended from a fixed point by a thread with negligible mass. Air resistance is also negligible.

The pendulum begins to oscillate from rest. Assume that the motion of the system is simple harmonic, and in one vertical plane. Fig. 1.1 shows the variation of kinetic energy of the pendulum bob with time.

![ib-9-1-sq-q1a-1](assets/019-ib-9-1-sq-q1a-1.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Determine the time period of the pendulum.
parts.solution_md:
The time period of the pendulum is:

![ib-9-1-sq-q1a-ms-1](assets/020-ib-9-1-sq-q1a-ms-1.png)

- 4.5 s **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

> *The time period is the time taken for **one full oscillation** of the pendulum. This can be read from the graph. Make sure to always check the units on the time axis before stating your final answer! In this case it is in seconds (s) but many graphs often have milliseconds (ms) instead.*

> *Remember that for a graph of kinetic energy, one full oscillation from the equilibrium position contains three peaks. Kinetic energy is at a maximum as the pendulum passes the equilibrium position. Therefore, for one complete oscillation, kinetic energy will begin at maximum, dip to zero at amplitude, peak at maximum as it passes through equilibrium, dip to zero at the opposite amplitude, and then return to maximum as it returns to equilibrium position.*

A small metal pendulum bob is suspended from a fixed point by a thread with negligible mass. Air resistance is also negligible. The pendulum begins to oscillate from rest. Assume that the motion of the system is simple harmonic, and in one vertical plane. Fig. 1.1 shows the variation of kinetic energy of the pendulum bob with time.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

A small metal pendulum bob is suspended from a fixed point by a thread with negligible mass. Air resistance is also negligible. The pendulum begins to oscillate from rest. Assume that the motion of the system is simple harmonic, and in one vertical plane. Fig. 1.1 shows the variation of kinetic energy of the pendulum bob with time. Fig. 1.1 (graph shows maximum kinetic energy of 20 mJ)

The mass of the pendulum bob is 60 × 10<sup>–3</sup> kg.

i) Determine the maximum kinetic energy of the pendulum bob.

[1]

ii) Show that the maximum speed of the bob is about 0.82 m s<sup>–1</sup>.

[3]
parts.solution_md:
(i) The maximum kinetic energy of the bob is:

- 20 mJ **OR **20 × 10<sup>–3</sup> J  (from the graph) **[1 mark]**

(ii) The maximum speed of the bob is:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of the bob, *m *=* *60 × 10<sup>–3</sup> kg
- Kinetic energy of the bob, *E*<sub>k</sub> = 20 mJ = 20 × 10<sup>–3</sup> J

Rearrange the kinetic energy equation for the speed, *v:*

- $E_{K}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$
- $2E_{K}=mv^{2}$
- *v* = $\sqrt{\frac{2E_{k}}{m}}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the values into the speed equation:

parts.problem_md:
The amplitude of the pendulum is 60 cm when it swings with a frequency of 0.7 Hz. During this oscillation, the maximum kinetic energy of the pendulum is 23 J.

Determine the mass of the pendulum bob.
parts.solution_md:
To determine the mass of the pendulum bob:

List the known quantities:

- Amplitude, $A=x_{0}=60\mathrm{cm}=0.6m$
- Frequency, $f=0.7\mathrm{Hz}$
- Maximum kinetic energy, $E_{Kmax}=23J$

Recall the total energy equation and rearrange to solve for *m*:

- $E=\frac{1}{2}mω^{2}x_{0}^{2}$
- $m=\frac{2E}{ω^{2}x_{0}^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the equation for angular velocity into the total energy equation:

- $ω=\frac{2π}{T}=2πf$
- $m = \frac{2 E}{( 2 \mathrm{\pi } f )^{2} x_{0}^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in the known values to calculate mass:

- $E_{Kmax}=E$ **[1 mark]**
- $m = \frac{2 \times 23}{( 2 \mathrm{\pi } \times 0.7 )^{2} \times ( 0.6 )^{2}}$
- $m=6.6\mathrm{kg}$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

**Extract:**

The amplitude of the pendulum is 60 cm when it swings with a frequency of 0.7 Hz. During this oscillation, the maximum kinetic energy of the pendulum is 23 J.
Determine the mass of the pendulum bob. (m = 6.6 kg)

Calculate the kinetic energy of the pendulum when the pendulum bob is at a distance of $0.4x_{0}$ from its point of maximum displacement.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the kinetic energy of the pendulum bob:

List the known quantities:

- Maximum kinetic energy, $E_{Kmax}=\frac{1}{2}mω^{2}x_{0}^{2}=23J$ (from part (b))
- Amplitude, $A=x_{0}=0.6m$ (from part (a))
- Frequency, $f=0.7\mathrm{Hz}$ (from part (a))
- Mass of pendulum, $m=6.6\mathrm{kg}$ (from part (b))

Determine the displacement from the equilibrium position:

- The question states that the pendulum is $0.4x_{0}$ from its maximum displacement ![9-1-hl-mcq-m5-ms](assets/023-9-1-hl-mcq-m5-ms.jpg)

  - Therefore, it is $0.6x_{0}$ from its equilibrium position **OR** $x=0.6\times0.6=0.36m$ **[1 mark]**

Using the kinetic energy equation to determine the kinetic energy at this displacement:

- $E_{K } = 1 \frac{1}{2} m \\omega ^{2} ( x_{0}^{2} - x^{2} ) = 1 \frac{1}{2} m ( 2 \pi f )^{2} ( x_{0}^{2} - x^{2} )$
- $E_{K } = 1 \frac{1}{2} \times 6.6 \times ( 2 \pi \times 0.7 )^{2} \times ( 0.6^{2} - 0.36^{2} )$ **[1 mark]**
- $E_{K}=14.72J$** [1 mark]**

**OR**

- $E_{K } = 1 \frac{1}{2} m \\omega ^{2} ( x_{0}^{2} - x^{2} ) = 1 \frac{1}{2} m \\omega ^{2} ( x_{0}^{2} - ( 0.6 x_{0} )^{2} )$
- $E_{K } = 1 \frac{1}{2} m \\omega ^{2} x_{0}^{2} ( 1 - 0.6^{2} ) = 23 ( 1 - 0.6^{2} )$ **[1 mark]**

- $E_{K}=14.72J$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *We can use the total energy equation in this instance because we know the value of the maximum kinetic energy which is equal to the total energy of the system. Always choose equations based on the known quantities you are given (or can calculate from what you are given!)*

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

A U shaped tube with cross-sectional area A contains a liquid of mass m, density ρ and volume V as shown in Fig. 1.1. When the water of length L is in equilibrium in the tube the levels of water on either side are equal. When the water is pushed down a distance x_max on one side of the tube then the water on the opposite side rises. Upon release the water undergoes simple harmonic motion as the water levels on each side rise and fall about the equilibrium position.
E_k(max) = 1/2 ALρ(v_max)^2 (From part a)
E_p(max) = Aρg(x_max)^2 (From part b)

Show that the time period of the oscillation of the liquid in the U shaped tube of Fig. 1.1 is given by the equation

$T=2π\sqrt{\frac{l}{2g}}$
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- $E_{k ( m a x )} = 1 \frac{1}{2} A L \\rho v_{m a x}^{2}$ (From part a))
- *E*<sub>*p (max)*</sub> = *Aρgx*<sub>*max*</sub><sup>*2 *</sup>(From part b))

Combine the expressions and rearrange to get an expression for $\frac{x_{max}}{v_{max}}$:

- $\frac{1}{2}ALρv_{max}^{2}=Aρgx_{max}^{2}$
- $\frac{v_{max}^{2}}{x_{max}^{2}}=\frac{2Aρg}{ALρ}$
- $\frac{v_{max}^{2}}{x_{max}^{2}}=\frac{2g}{L}$
- $\frac{v_{max}}{x_{max}}=\sqrt{\frac{2g}{L}}$
- $\frac{x_{max}}{v_{max}}=\sqrt{\frac{L}{2g}}$ **[1 mark]**

Use the equation for *v*<sub>*max*</sub> to substitute in for *ω*:

- Recall: *v*<sub>*max *</sub>= *ωx*<sub>*max *</sub>(for amplitude *x*<sub>*max*</sub>)
- $ω=\frac{v_{max}}{x_{max}}$ $\rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{ω}=\frac{x_{max}}{v_{max}}$
- $\frac{1}{ω}=\sqrt{\frac{L}{2g}}$ **[1 mark]**

Recall the equation for angular velocity, *ω *in terms of time period *T *and obtain the required equation:

- Recall: $ω=\frac{2π}{T}$
- So, $\frac{1}{ω}=\frac{T}{2π}$
- $\frac{T}{2π}=\sqrt{\frac{L}{2g}}$ **[1 mark]**
- So, $T=2π\sqrt{\frac{L}{2g}}$

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *You do not need to know this equation for your course, so don't learn it. These types of hard questions are common when they take you beyond the syllabus. *

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

A mass-spring system oscillates with simple harmonic motion. The graph in Fig. 1.1 shows how the potential energy of the spring varies with displacement. (ii) the total energy of the system. Mark scheme: The graph shows that the total energy is 40 mJ.
(ii) the potential energy in the spring when the displacement is x = 0.1 m. Mark scheme: The potential energy at x = 0.1 m is 9 mJ.

Determine the kinetic energy of the mass-spring system at *x* = 0.1 m.
parts.solution_md:
Determine the kinetic energy of the mass-spring system at *x* = 0.1 m:

List the known quantities:

- Total energy, $E$ = 40 mJ (from part a)
- Potential energy at x = 0.1 m, $E_{P}$ = 9 mJ (from part b)

Determine an expression for *E*<sub>K</sub>:

- Energy in a system in SHM is conserved
- So, total energy:  $E=E_{K}+E_{P}$
- Therefore, kinetic energy:  $E_{K}=E-E_{P}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the kinetic energy at *x* = 0.1 m:

- $E_{K}$ = 40 − 9 = 31 mJ** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

equations.alt: E space equals space E subscript K space plus space E subscript P
E subscript K space equals space E space minus space E subscript P

parts.problem_md:
The block used in the same mass-spring system has a mass of 25 g. The maximum kinetic energy of the block is 40 mJ.

Calculate the maximum velocity of the oscillating block
parts.solution_md:
Calculate the maximum velocity of the oscillation:

List the known quantities:

- Maximum kinetic energy, *E* = *E*<sub>*K max*</sub> = 40 mJ = 0.04 J
- Mass *m* = 25 g = 0.025 kg

Recall and rearrange the kinetic energy equation to solve for *v:*

- $E_{K}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$
- *v* = $\sqrt{\frac{2E_{K}}{m}}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the velocity:

- v = $\sqrt{\frac{2\times0.04}{0.025}}$ = 1.8 m s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

equations.alt: E subscript K space equals space 1 half m v squared
